doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Melody and form in his writing
summary: The 16-17-16 form and why he writes the melody first and lets it dictate structure.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It’s got a couple of sections to it. It goes into a swing thing eventually.
It takes everybody out because it’s like 16-17-16, that’s the form.
Oh. There’s no coasting on it.
Oh no, no. That 17th bar will get you if you’re not on it. And then there’s a one-two bar. [scats]. That part [scats] that’s a one-two [scats].
Did you do that because you had a melody going and you needed to put it in let’s call it an odd measure to accommodate the melody?

Yeah. Because to me, the melody is the strongest thing. I mean I think I write strong melodies because I concentrate on the melodies. Melodies are what makes a song. I mean you could have chords going but the chords — I prefer to write a melody before I write the structure. It dictates the structure, as far as I’m concerned. Because in the end it’s the melody that the people are going to be whistling walking down the street. And a lot of people have told me that they wake up in the middle of the night whistling some of my songs. If I didn’t write in that way, I don’t know if they would whistle somebody’s rhythms. Something about melody, it changes you.
That’s a great compliment I think when people say, “You know that tune you wrote, I just got it in my head.”
